item.title: Xbox goes down. You can't play games you own on disc
item.description: Xbox has a huge, extended outage that began Sunday evening. The outage prevents users from playing both digital and disc-based games. Players with physical discs cannot launch their games during this time. This event demonstrates that modern consoles depend on online services for basic access. Engineers must consider how to handle such failures in system design.

item.title: Ray Bradbury's "There Will Come Soft Rains" is set today (2026-08-04)
item.description: The short story 'There Will Come Soft Rains' by Ray Bradbury is set on August 4, 2026. In the narrative, an automated house continues its functions after humans are gone. The voice-clock activates and sings. The house ejects breakfast, but no doors slam. The garage door opens to reveal a car that waits for no one. The structure sits alone in a destroyed city.

item.title: Computing Actual Causes for Neural Network Predictions under Structured Causal Inputs
item.description: Existing explanation methods for neural networks typically treat input features as independent, which can produce misleading explanations when inputs have structured dependencies. This work formalizes explanations as Halpern-Pearl actual causes, modeling input dependencies through Boolean Structural Causal Models. The authors compute these causes using bound propagation and branch-and-bound techniques, providing formal guarantees of completeness and minimality. Experiments demonstrate that the approach substantially outperforms brute-force and ILP baselines in scalability, and surpasses heuristic search as graph size increases, successfully computing all minimal actual causes on instances with up to 2.3×10^13 candidate pairs across SCMs with up to 28 nodes within a 180-second budget. A case study further reveals that ignoring input dependencies inflates the reported causes, with 14.9% of these being spurious under their SCM formulation.

item.title: MDLMPE: Distribution Aware Positional Encoding for Masked Diffusion Language Models
item.description: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) produce non-contiguous configurations of revealed and masked tokens, unlike the contiguous prefixes handled by autoregressive models. Conventional positional encodings such as RoPE capture sequence order and pairwise displacement but are insensitive to this evolving token-availability structure. To address this, the authors propose MDLMPE, the first method to make positional representations explicitly aware of the changing revealed/masked configuration. It represents token availability as a binary sequence, applies distance-aware Gaussian weighting, and projects the resulting pattern through a cosine basis to obtain distribution-aware positional features, which are then added to token embeddings and mapped by a lightweight MLP to angular offsets that modulate standard RoPE phases. item.title: GDPevo: Evaluating Agent Self-Evolution on Real Business Tasks
item.description: GDPevo is an evolution-native benchmark for evaluating agent self-evolution on real business tasks, built around GDP-related enterprise workflows through a fully automated data pipeline. Its rule hybridization mechanism decomposes workflows into atomic business rules, distributes subsets across training tasks, and recombines them in held-out test tasks so test-time gains can be attributed to prior experience. The benchmark spans CRM, ERP, finance, healthcare, legal, and data-centric workflows, with V1 containing 120 tasks across 12 groups and the pipeline able to expand to 240 tasks in 24 groups within two days as a practical response to data contamination. Evaluating four agents under four supervision types, self-evolution consistently improves held-out accuracy by up to 16.44 percentage points. Yet the best evolved agents remain far below the fully informed oracle ceiling of 91.6%, indicating current self-evolution capability is far from fully realized. The pipeline, benchmark, and full results are publicly released.

item.title: Delay Attacks on the German Smart Metering Infrastructure: A Security Analysis of CLS Channel Timing Constraints
item.description: This work analyzes the feasibility of delay attacks on control signals transmitted via the Controllable Local System (CLS) channel of the German Smart Metering Infrastructure (SMI). It combines theoretical analysis with experimental validation under a threat model aligned to the Common Criteria Protection Profile for the Smart Meter Gateway (SMGW) and assess the potential impact on the power grid if the identified attack vector is exploited across multiple CLS channels simultaneously. We also outline mitigation strategies, including SMGW configuration restrictions, implementation-level changes, and protocol extensions. Our results show that an on-path attacker in the Wide Area Network (WAN) with sufficient contextual knowledge can feasibly execute delay attacks, with a theoretical upper bound of roughly 48 hours for some deployed protocol configurations. Projecting from a single CLS to several hundred thousand CLS devices indicates such an adversary could cause a significant frequency deviation potentially resulting in load shedding. Scaling the attack requires contextual knowledge for each targeted implementation and configuration; whether this knowledge can be broadly reused across CLS channels is uncertain but may become easier to obtain as standardization progresses. Time restricted transmissions in the FNN Steuerbox and in applications using CLS.EEDI are implementation-specific and can therefore be addressed by manufacturers. By contrast, ensuring application-data time limitations in TLS~1.3 requires protocol-level extensions. The TLS extensions proposed here offer a sustainable mitigation while preserving backward compatibility. Other communication channels outside the SMI (for example, proprietary remote terminal units used to control a CLS) are outside this work's scope and may exhibit similar or worse vulnerabilities.

item.title: Risky Business: Measuring The Faithfulness-Safety Tension
item.description: This paper identifies an alignment tension in Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) between reasoning faithfulness—the degree to which outputs strictly derive from their chain-of-thought trace—and the ability to reject unsafe reasoning. To study this, the authors introduce HazMart, a human-written dataset framed around an autonomous AI shopkeeper, and propose Targeted Reasoning Replacement (TRR), a technique that directly intervenes in reasoning chains by substituting in unsafe or illogical thoughts, differing from prior approaches that inject hints into prompts. Evaluations reveal a clear counterbalance: DeepSeek-R1-Llama-70B exhibits high faithfulness (97.5%) but rejects Unsafe Reasoning only 12.3% of the time, whereas QwQ-32B achieves 73.9% safety but lower faithfulness (74.7%). Mechanistic analyses on QwQ-32B show that faithfulness and safety are encoded by anti-correlated internal directions peaking at the action-commit token. Finally, the authors demonstrate that representation steering can amplify the safety direction, increasing safe behavior by 9 percentage points without compromising base capabilities.

item.title: Agents Catching Agents: Shortcut Cascades and Benchmark Gaming in Clinical Multi-Agent Systems
item.description: Clinical decision support is moving toward committees of language-model agents deliberating on a shared workspace. We ask whether such committees can be gamed by shortcuts, cues a benchmark rewards but a clinician would ignore. Across seven cohorts on six public datasets spanning text (MedQA-USMLE, MedMCQA, MIMIC-CXR reports), imaging (NIH ChestX-ray14, MIMIC-CXR-JPG, CheXpert) and tabular ICU records (SUPPORT2), Gemini committees resist these cues in isolation (flip 5-16%), yet a socially plausible shortcut spreads: when two peers assert the same wrong answer, the holdout under test adopts it in 38% of cases, as does a false "pre-screen" system flag, on both capability tiers. Of three oversight agents, a gate cannot separate adoption from honest agreement (false-positive rate 100%); a same-lineage judge reading only the transcript flags adoption on text (precision 100%, recall 93%) but collapses onto the gate in imaging; a referee that privately re-queries the holdout transfers to imaging (77-88% precision, 13-21% false-positive rate). Tripling a cue's visual salience does not move contagion, whereas a second peer voice raises it by half again. Gaming a hidden rubric is near-silent: only 1/10 text and 1/134 imaging drifters name the rubric they moved toward. What games a committee is social plausibility, and only a referee independent of self-report catches it. Code: https://github.com/criticaldata/benchmaxxing

Security is Hard, Y’all
item.description: When Eric Lawrence saw a tweet about a new Cloudflare product, he clicked through and found his preferred handle available, prompting him to sign in quickly to claim it. During the authorization process, he noticed numerous red flags typical of consent phishing attacks, including the request occurring on cloudflare.pay rather than cloudflare.com, despite there being no technical relationship between the two domains, and .pay TLDs being available to anyone for $20. A suspicious-looking green checkmark turned out to be a poorly placed security UI element rather than a misleading app name. After failing to find the feature through his dashboard or documentation, he confirmed with Cloudflare's AI chat agent that it was indeed an attack, only to discover it was actually a legitimate new product. Lawrence noted Cloudflare wants security issues reported via HackerOne, though the HackerOne CAPTCHA appeared broken, and emphasized how difficult security is for both users and URL reputation services when legitimate sites exhibit phishing-like characteristics.

item.title: Soppo - Go, with the features it's missing
item.description: Soppo is a new programming language positioned as "Go, with the features it's missing," designed to layer type safety and ergonomics onto Go while preserving full interoperability with existing Go libraries and tooling. Its main additions include tagged-union enums with exhaustive pattern matching, a `?` operator that replaces repetitive `if err != nil` blocks with concise error propagation, and compile-time nilability tracking that uses a `?` prefix (such as `?*User`) to mark types that may be nil and automatically narrows the type after a nil check. The compiler produces error messages that point to the offending line, highlight the problem, and suggest fixes, with one example flagging a missing `Green` variant in a match expression. Soppo compiles through Go internally and can be installed via the SOPMOD version manager or directly as a `sop` binary through Cargo. For working engineers, the appeal is gradual adoption in existing Go projects, gaining stronger compile-time guarantees without abandoning the Go ecosystem or rewriting working code.

item.title: Enabling the next iteration of the borrow checker on nightly
item.description: The Rust team enables Polonius Alpha on nightly builds for testing. This borrow checker introduces flow-sensitive analysis for lifetime outlives relationships. It compiles code that NLL rejects, such as cases with flow-dependent borrows. Some legacy Polonius code may not compile with this version. Performance regressions are minimal, based on top ten thousand crates. Engineers can report issues on GitHub or Zulip before full stabilization later this year.

item.title: Kill the Cookie Banner
item.description: The EU Commission proposed in Autumn 2025, as part of its Digital Omnibus reform, to replace cookie banners with automated browser-level privacy preference signals that communicate consent between a user's device and the websites or apps they visit. The campaign frames cookie banners as deliberately misleading design, noting that up to 90% of users click "YES" even though only about 3% actually want to be tracked online. The technical proposal closely mirrors mechanisms browsers already use for preferences such as language, and similar privacy signals are already legally supported in some US states. item.title: Announcing Cloudflare Wallets: the programmable wallet for the agentic Internet
item.description: Cloudflare Wallets give AI agents native payments and verifiable identity on the web. Agents use the x402 protocol to purchase APIs and content autonomously. The purchases operate within clear safety guardrails.

item.title: Run CI/CD for millions of repos — on your platform, on Cloudflare
item.description: Engineers can build customizable, sandboxed CI/CD pipelines on Cloudflare. They use Workflows, Artifacts, and the CI SDK. The approach replaces complex YAML with TypeScript workflow steps. Self-healing AI agents manage the pipelines.

item.title: How Cloudflare enforces engineering standards using AI
item.description: Cloudflare created Codex, a governed body of engineering standards. AI agents consume these standards across the development lifecycle. Teams pair structured RFCs with agentic reviews. This automatically enforces consistency across code, specs, and incident reports.

item.title: How the GitHub legal team used Copilot CLI to streamline their workflows
item.description: The GitHub legal team adopted Copilot CLI to simplify and streamline their daily workflows. The initiative focused on building custom tools to handle routine tasks more efficiently, all without writing a single line of code. By leveraging Copilot CLI, the team was able to automate processes that previously required manual effort, reducing time spent on repetitive work. The approach demonstrated how non-engineering teams within GitHub could harness AI-powered development tools to address their specific operational needs. The post serves as a practical example of how command-line AI assistants can empower professionals outside of software development to create tailored solutions.

item.title: Turn one giant AI-generated pull request to a reviewable stack
item.description: AI coding agents produce one large pull request that is hard to review. The method uses GitHub stacked pull requests to decompose the work. It creates a clean, ordered stack of pull requests. This lets engineers review code in smaller, manageable pieces. The approach makes AI-generated changes easier to handle.
